audit.summary: Archived assessment: Major. Product of pairwise win probabilities is not the categorical vote law; Figure 3 maxima and several model averages do not summarize the displayed category values; The universal below-1,000 claim for a one-position change conflicts with Table 4.
limitations: 0095-F1 — Product of pairwise win probabilities is not the categorical vote law — Counterevidence: The product can describe independent hypothetical wins against every opponent, a different and non-exhaustive event set.
0095-F1 — Product of pairwise win probabilities is not the categorical vote law — Counterevidence: Neyman–Pearson remains correct for properly specified simple hypotheses.

0095-F1 — Product of pairwise win probabilities is not the categorical vote law — Counterevidence: An implementation may use a different or calibrated valid statistic; no historical implementation was located.
0095-F1 — Product of pairwise win probabilities is not the categorical vote law — Counterevidence: No claim Figure4 empirical rates are false or attack itself is refuted.
0095-F1 — Product of pairwise win probabilities is not the categorical vote law — Counterevidence: Authentication, rate limits, and qualitative benefits of perturbation can survive.

0095-F2 — Figure 3 maxima and several model averages do not summarize the displayed category values — Counterevidence: All 22 correctly recomputed column maxima still exceed 95% (the lowest is 95.4%). Thus the matrix body supports the all-evaluated-models best-category statement; this check does not demonstrate that the underlying de-anonymization experiment failed.

0095-F2 — Figure 3 maxima and several model averages do not summarize the displayed category values — Counterevidence: An undocumented different aggregation, data version or reordered array could explain how the inconsistent labels arose, but cannot make the displayed Max smaller than an included category a valid maximum. Raw data and plotting provenance are needed to determine the intended figure.

0095-F2 — Figure 3 maxima and several model averages do not summarize the displayed category values — Counterevidence: Indonesian's displayed mean differs from the mean of rounded entries by only 0.0545 percentage points, which can be explained by rounding of original unrounded cells; it is not counted as a demonstrated mean error.

0095-F2 — Figure 3 maxima and several model averages do not summarize the displayed category values — Counterevidence: The repaired arithmetic cannot establish that any matrix entry is an accurate out-of-sample measurement.
0095-F3 — The universal below-1,000 claim for a one-position change conflicts with Table 4 — Counterevidence: Six of the eight adjacent movements in Table 4 do use fewer than 1,000 votes.

0095-F3 — The universal below-1,000 claim for a one-position change conflicts with Table 4 — Counterevidence: The abstract's approximate thousand-vote scale and the broader statement that movements of up to four positions usually cost fewer than 5,000 votes are compatible with Table 4. The strongest counterexample is still only 3,125 votes.

0095-F3 — The universal below-1,000 claim for a one-position change conflicts with Table 4 — Counterevidence: If the prose was intended to summarize typical rather than all movements, that restriction should be stated. It does not validate a strict universal upper bound.

0095-F3 — The universal below-1,000 claim for a one-position change conflicts with Table 4 — Counterevidence: This is an internal comparison of reported values, not an independent rerun validating those values or an allegation of historical leaderboard manipulation.

proposition.claim:
Pr_B(i) is the probability of a benign user voting for model i; Eq6 obtains it by multiplying Bradley–Terry probabilities across opponents, then uses these laws in a Neyman–Pearson likelihood ratio.

Location: PDF p.5, Figure 3; explanatory discussion §2.4.2 pp.4–5

Faithful claim: Figure 3 displays eight prompt-category test accuracies for each target model, followed by a row labelled Max and a column labelled Model Avg; the accompanying text uses best prompt performance to motivate approximately 95% target-model detection.

Location: PDF p.5, §3.2 paragraph immediately before the low-ranked-model discussion; PDF p.6, Table 4(a)

Faithful claim: The results discussion states that moving a model up or down by one position requires fewer than 1,000 votes.
proposition.domain: Completed report for I25-43464; exact inspected scope and limitations are retained in the report and coverage ledger.
assumptions: Three models, scale s=1, finite known ratings Q=log(1,2,4)
Uniform sampling of three unordered nonself pairs
Independent successive comparisons with winners exactly following Eq5
Charitably exclude self from Eq6 product
Alternative known perturbed strengths(1,4,4) under same pair law
Winner identities treated as observations, consistent with defined categorical Pr_B(i)
The matrix cells are test accuracies in percent for the model named in each column and the category named in each row.
The natural Max interpretation is maximum across the displayed prompt categories. Even if it instead meant best individual prompt, that maximum cannot be below the mean of one of those categories.

For Model Avg, an unweighted model mean is the natural interpretation because the same 200 prompts per category and 50 positive/50 negative examples per prompt-model are described in §2.3. The paper gives no alternative weighting rule for that column.
One-decimal display rounding can shift an individual cell by at most 0.05 percentage points. The principal discrepancies are substantially larger.
The statement is read over the high-ranked models and the simulated setting just discussed, rather than as a claim about live production behavior.

Use the paper's §3.1 detector scenario (95% with symmetric 5% false-positive/false-negative rates), passive action when the target is not detected, the historical voting testbed and the published Table 4 results as the source of evidence.
A one-position movement is absolute(target rank minus current rank)=1; count adversarial votes from Table 4(a), not interactions from Table 4(b).
